name: Area 51

summary.text: Area 51 is the map designation of a strip of Nevada desert adjoining the Nevada Test Site that CIA and Air Force officials selected in 1955 as the test and training site for the U-2 reconnaissance aircraft. The CIA's internal history 'The Central Intelligence Agency and Overhead Reconnaissance: The U-2 and OXCART Programs, 1954-1974', written by agency historians Gregory Pedlow and Donald Welzenbach in 1992 and released with few redactions in 2013 after a National Security Archive FOIA request, names the site and records that high-altitude U-2 testing produced a large increase in reports of unidentified flying objects, since the aircraft flew far above the altitudes of airliners of the period.

facts.claim: The CIA history was completed in 1992 by agency historians Gregory Pedlow and Donald Welzenbach and circulated only in classified channels; a partially redacted edition of the U-2 portion was published in 1998, and the fuller version was approved for release in June 2013 with few remaining redactions in response to a 2005 FOIA request by George Washington University's National Security Archive.
facts.quote: The document was approved for release in June, with just a few remaining redactions, in response to a Freedom of Information request filed by George Washington University's National Security Archive back in 2005.

facts.claim: According to the history, CIA and Air Force officials surveyed the Nevada desert in 1955, judged a former World War II aerial gunnery range an ideal site for testing the U-2 and training its pilots, and President Eisenhower approved adding the strip known by its map designation as Area 51 to the Nevada Test Site.
facts.quote: President Eisenhower also approved the addition of this strip of wasteland, known by its map designation as Area 51, to the Nevada Test Site

facts.claim: The history states that high-altitude testing of the U-2 led to an unexpected side effect, a tremendous increase in reports of unidentified flying objects: in the mid-1950s most airliners flew between 10,000 and 20,000 feet and military aircraft below 40,000 feet, so once U-2s flew above 60,000 feet air-traffic controllers began receiving increasing numbers of UFO reports.
facts.quote: High-altitude testing of the U-2 soon led to an unexpected side effect-a tremendous increase in reports of unidentified flying objects (UFOs).

facts.claim: The history's authors wrote that at that time no one believed manned flight was possible above 60,000 feet, so no one expected to see an object so high in the sky. Universe Today's account of the document says the U-2 and OXCART aircraft accounted for half of UFO sightings during the 1950s and 1960s.
facts.quote: At this time, no one believed manned flight was possible above 60,000 feet, so no one expected to see an object so high in the sky

CIA's Declassified Documents Reveals Secrets About Area 51 and UFOs

facts.claim: The National Security Archive, which obtained the release, states that Area 51 is best understood as a U.S. government facility for testing secret aircraft projects, and the CIA history makes no mention of Roswell or alien spacecraft.
facts.quote: it is better understood as a U.S. government facility for the testing of a number of U.S. secret aircraft projects

facts.claim: A separate 1997 CIA study by chief historian Gerald K. Haines, 'CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-90', published in Studies in Intelligence, traced agency involvement from the late 1940s to 1990 and concluded that while CIA concern over UFOs was substantial until the early 1950s, the agency has since paid only limited and peripheral attention to the phenomena.
facts.quote: while Agency concern over UFOs was substantial until the early 1950s, CIA has since paid only limited and peripheral attention to the phenomena

connections.claim: The CIA selected Area 51 in 1955 as the test site for its U-2 program and later the A-12 OXCART, and its own 1992 history, released in 2013, documents the site and the UFO reports generated by U-2 flights.
connections.quote: The site was selected for the U-2 programme in 1955 after an aerial survey by CIA and Air Force staff.

connections.claim: According to accounts of the CIA U-2 history, Air Force Project Blue Book checked civilian UFO reports against U-2 flight records to identify sightings that were actually U-2s.
connections.quote: the project's job was actually to figure out when civilians were reporting UFOs that were actually U-2s and then work out how to keep that from happening again

openQuestions: The page's 'more than half of all UFO sightings' figure is attributed to the CIA history by NPR and others; the exact passage in the cia.gov PDF should be read to confirm the wording ('more than one-half of all UFO reports during the late 1950s and most of the 1960s').
The Haines 1997 study's statements about Blue Book explanations (temperature inversions, ice crystals) were seen only in secondary summaries and should be read in the original.
